A four year old sits alone in a room with one marshmallow.
She can eat it now. Or wait fifteen minutes, and get two.
That tiny choice became one of the most famous experiments in psychology.
And it says something uncomfortable about your money.
In the late nineteen sixties, researchers at Stanford gave hundreds of kids this exact deal.
Some kids ate the marshmallow in seconds.
Others sang, covered their eyes, even kicked the table, anything to wait.
Years later, the researchers checked in on them.
The kids who waited had, on average, higher test scores and handled stress better.
Here's the strange part.
Newer studies found the effect is much smaller than people thought.
Family money and trust explained a lot of it.
If you grow up with promises that get broken, eating the marshmallow now is the smart move.
Now look at your bank account.
Every paycheck is a marshmallow.
Spend it now, and you feel great for a day.
Wait, and something strange happens.
Say you put away two hundred dollars a month.
At seven percent a year, after thirty years, that's about two hundred and forty thousand dollars.
You only put in seventy two thousand.
The rest is the second marshmallow.
So how do you wait, when everything around you says eat it now?
Number one. Hide the marshmallow.
The kids who waited best didn't stare at it. They looked away.
Move your savings to an account you never see.
Number two. Make waiting automatic.
Set the transfer for payday, before you can change your mind.
Number three. Trust the deal.
Waiting only works when you believe the second marshmallow is real.
Start small, so you can watch it grow.
Two people earn the same salary.
One spends every raise. The other saves half of it.
Ten years later, they live on different planets.
And it all started with one small choice.
Eat it now, or wait for two.
